solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: reproduced suggests the letters are made again in a new form, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that great art is being churned out in cheap copies.
explanation.definitionFit: Something classic is the perfect model or typical example of its kind, the sense of a typical specimen.

clue.text: Tight young lady narrowly avoided collision

definitions.note: a noun phrase here: an incident where a crash was only just escaped

parts.note: tight means stingy, as does near in old British usage
Miss is the title of a young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A tipsy young woman just escapes a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' looks like 'drunk' but means mean with money, an old British sense of NEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names an incident in which two vehicles or aircraft very nearly hit each other.

indicators.note: about means going round, so the letters S and ME surround the revolutionary

parts.note: me (or mi) is the third note of the sol-fa scale
Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary

explanation.surface: A second memo about a revolutionary's plot.
explanation.walkthrough: The revolutionary is Che Guevara, a crossword favourite; 'note' is a sol-fa syllable, not a written memo.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot and a scheme are both secret plans, so these are synonyms.

clue.text: Popular novel I wrote gets to me

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a novel I wrote would be my book

explanation.surface: An author is pleased that their bestselling novel is getting through to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases introduce a personal opinion, an idiom meaning in my view.

indicators.note: ignored says this letter is left out of the word

parts.note: the most obese is the fattest

explanation.surface: A report that evidence about the heaviest woman was disregarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignored' drops F from FATTEST. 'evidence' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To evidence something is to bear witness to it or prove it, a verb synonym.

parts.note: Conference is a popular British variety of pear, and pear with this soft French cheese is a classic pairing; the answer is the cheese half

explanation.surface: Seems to ask about splitting a meeting, with cheese on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conference' looks like a meeting but is the pear variety; 'Half of' looks like a letter selection but means one partner of the pairing.
explanation.definitionFit: The soft French cheese is the other half of the well-known pear-and-cheese combination.

definitions.meaning: given without charge, as a drink a pub offers

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both unoccupied and costing nothing, two separate senses.

parts.note: chains are restraints or restrictions
tore means ripped, so damaged

explanation.surface: Red tape has hurt a shop's business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' looks like an anagram signal but is simply a synonym for TORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of shops under one ownership is a type of retail business.

parts.note: a booster is a follow-up vaccine dose, given by injection into the upper limb; the phrase also means any fillip

explanation.definitionFit: A vaccine top-up is literally an injection in the limb, and the idiom also means an encouraging boost.

clue.text: Awful rage after church makes accusation

indicators.note: after places the rearranged word following the church abbreviation
awful suggests the word is badly mangled, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fury after a church service leads to someone being accused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' reads as describing the rage but is the anagram signal; the shuffled letters come after the church abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is a formal allegation of wrongdoing, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Play that may bring tears to one's eyes?

definitions.meaning: Noel Coward's 1925 comedy of that name

definitions.text: that may bring tears to one's eyes?
definitions.meaning: the pollen allergy that makes eyes stream

explanation.walkthrough: The tearful reading suggests a tragedy, but the play is a comedy; the tears come from pollen.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a Coward comedy and also the common allergy to grass pollen causing watery eyes.

parts.note: a trident is a three-pronged spear

explanation.surface: A little spear with a sharp point.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp, harsh sound or voice is described as shrill and grating, a synonym.

indicators.note: wearing means the letters ONE are worn around the boy's name, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written
Tiny Tim is the small boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol

explanation.surface: A bright little boy dressed in a onesie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp' is used as in 'three o'clock sharp', not clever; Tiny Tim is the Dickens child.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving at three o'clock sharp means arriving punctually, an idiomatic synonym.

definitions.meaning: to lay down songs in a studio
an informal idiom for departing quickly

explanation.definitionFit: Laying down songs and hurrying off are both meanings of the phrase, literal and idiomatic.

clue.text: Maybe "Pass the Parcel" can be played after this!

definitions.text: Maybe "Pass the Parcel" can be played after this!

parts.words: Maybe "Pass the Parcel" can be played after this!
parts.note: Pass the Parcel is a children's party game; a delivery worker's rap at the door brings a parcel that can then be passed on, and the answer is also a party kissing game

explanation.walkthrough: Pass the Parcel and the answer are both traditional British party games; the joke is that a delivery must arrive before a parcel can be passed.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of an old parlour game and, literally, the delivery worker's rap at the door bringing a package.

clue.text: A pasta; sculptor feeding husband with one

indicators.note: feeding means going into, so the sculptor is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: man is husband, as in 'man and wife'
Sir Anthony Caro was a British sculptor
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An artist passes a dish of pasta to a husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' belongs to the definition; 'with' only joins husband and one.
explanation.definitionFit: The tube-shaped pasta is one example of the many kinds of pasta.

clue.text: A polenta prepared with little effort

indicators.note: prepared, as a cook prepares a dish, signals the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Polenta that was easy to make.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handed to you on a dish comes without effort, an idiom for easily obtained.

clue.text: Member of the clergy in vicious circle

indicators.note: vicious suggests the word is violently attacked and scrambled

explanation.surface: A clergyman caught up in a vicious circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vicious' rearranges CIRCLE; the phrase 'vicious circle' makes it hard to spot as a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest or minister is a churchman, the plain sense of the term.

clue.text: Put right about me, extremely doughty

parts.note: re means about or concerning
taken as written

indicators.note: extremely means taking the extreme letters, the first and last, of the following word

explanation.surface: Someone brave sets things right for the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: To fix or correct a fault is to rectify it, a verb synonym.

parts.note: hot means highly fashionable
pants is British slang for rubbish or nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea that shorts are fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: These are very brief, tight shorts worn by women, a kind of short trousers.

clue.text: Absentee, not wholly faithful worker in colony

indicators.note: not wholly means the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: true means loyal or faithful
an ant is a worker living in a colony

explanation.surface: A worker who is not completely loyal goes missing from the colony.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil skipping school without permission is someone absent, the typical case.

clue.text: A very English mass, with song and prayer

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for mass in physics
an aria is a solo song in opera

explanation.surface: A description of an English church service with hymns and prayers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mass' is not the church service but the physics symbol M.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hail Mary is a Catholic devotion addressed to the Virgin, also set to music.

parts.note: vie means to compete or struggle

explanation.surface: Someone wrestling with their faith.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion or point of view is what one believes, a synonym.

clue.text: Get rid of university don, almost all moved

indicators.note: moved signals the letters are shifted around into a new order
almost means the word is not quite complete, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A college lecturer is dismissed, with nearly everything shifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts ALL to AL; 'moved' rearranges DON plus AL to NLOAD.
explanation.definitionFit: To unload something unwanted is to dispose of it, an informal synonym.

parts.note: leading means guiding or directing
to man is to staff, as in manning a desk

explanation.surface: A star actor who also runs the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' is a verb here, giving MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The star male role in a play or film is the main performer, so a synonym.

definitions.meaning: to endure or put up with, as in 'I can't stand it'

explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both seizing something and enduring something, two distinct senses.
